original_question: Show that the CG and Lanczos algorithms do or do not behave similarly in finite precision arithmetic when used to solve a symmetric positive definite linear system. This will, of course, depend on the implementation of each method, so use standard good implementations of both.
target_in_paper: Problem 2.16 in Section 2.6, "Symmetric Krylov methods in finite precision arithmetic."
correct_elements: Your draft is already almost a verbatim restatement of the paper's official open problem. It correctly identifies the two algorithms being compared (CG and Lanczos), the regime (finite precision arithmetic), the task (solving a symmetric positive definite linear system), and the paper's explicit caveat that the answer depends on the implementation, so one should use standard good implementations.
missing_details: State the linear system explicitly as Ax = b, with A symmetric positive definite (intended as a real SPD matrix) and b given.
Specify that both algorithms are compared on the same starting data, e.g. the same initial guess x0, equivalently the same starting residual r0 = b − Ax0 for Lanczos.
Make explicit that Lanczos is being used as a linear-system solver for the same SPD system, not merely as an eigenvalue routine.

Clarify that the scope is the standard floating-point / finite-precision setting of Section 2.6; broader models with inexact matrix-vector products or inexact preconditioner application are deferred to Problem 2.18, not Problem 2.16.

If the question is to be fully stand-alone, include the exact-arithmetic motivation from the surrounding text: CG and Lanczos are equivalent in exact arithmetic, and CG can be viewed as computing the Cholesky factorization of the Lanczos tridiagonal matrix.

The paper does not formalize a single metric for 'behave similarly'; a faithful rewrite should preserve that openness rather than replace it by an invented narrower criterion such as only residual norms, only convergence rate, or only attainable accuracy.
refined_question: Let A ∈ R^{n×n} be symmetric positive definite, let b ∈ R^n, and fix an initial guess x0 (so the common starting residual is r0 = b − Ax0). Although CG and Lanczos are equivalent in exact arithmetic, determine whether standard good floating-point implementations of CG and of Lanczos, when both are used to solve Ax = b from the same starting data, must exhibit similar finite-precision behavior, or whether they can behave genuinely differently.
justification: This draft targets Problem 2.16, not a broader neighboring problem. The match is nearly exact: Problem 2.16 in Section 2.6 asks whether CG and Lanczos behave similarly in finite precision arithmetic when used to solve a symmetric positive definite linear system, explicitly adding that one should use standard good implementations (p. 17). The immediately preceding discussion in the same section supplies the intended hidden context: CG and Lanczos are equivalent in exact arithmetic, CG may be interpreted as computing the Cholesky factorization of the tridiagonal matrix generated by Lanczos, and the unresolved issue is whether that relationship survives finite precision (pp. 16-17). I therefore kept the refinement narrow and did not broaden it to Problem 2.15 on recursively updated residuals dropping below machine precision, Problem 2.17 on the number of bits needed for a backward-error guarantee, or Problem 2.18 on more general inexact matrix-vector and preconditioner models.
